claims.text: Existing eutectic high-entropy alloys commonly have lamellar or straight rod-like multiphase microstructures.
A multi-objective data-driven optimization framework can coordinate composition, processing, mechanical testing, and microstructural characterization for EHEA development.
Iterative statistical or machine-learning guidance can produce controlled lamellar or vermicular EHEA microstructures.
Composition and thermomechanical processing can be used to tailor eutectic morphology.
Lamellar or vermicular morphologies can optimize the coexistence of hard and soft phases.
Mixtures of soft and hard eutectic phases can provide a balanced strength-ductility synergy.
A kinked vermicular eutectic microstructure can outperform straight eutectic morphologies in strength-ductility synergy.
Hierarchical constraints in a tailored lamellar EHEA can improve its mechanical response during deformation.
Tailored EHEA microstructures can arrest microcracks.
Control of phase fraction and lamellar spacing will beneficially constrain dislocation motion.
Control of phase fraction and lamellar spacing will impede crack propagation and thereby improve fracture toughness.
The optimized alloys will have approximately 10–20% higher yield strength than current eutectic HEAs.
The optimized alloys will have significantly higher fracture toughness than representative baseline eutectic HEAs.
The strength and fracture-resistance improvements will occur without sacrificing ductility.
The strength and fracture-resistance improvements will occur without sacrificing Young’s modulus.
Conventional straight eutectic morphologies restrict the scope for further mechanical-property improvement.
The approach requires microstructural and phase stability under intended service temperatures and loads.
Unwanted intermetallic formation or uncontrolled coarsening can disrupt the proposed property synergy.
Interactions among alloying elements and processing pathways may reduce the attainable improvements.
